\chapter{The Throat Row and the Palate Row}
\label{ch:two-rows-runway}
\hlchaptermodality{6}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can write seven more consonants and say, for any of them, whether the voice is on and whether the breath is released.}

Say both four-step rows in order from the two switches that generate them, with no model on the page.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[kha]{\mr{ख} — \emph{ka} with the breath let out}

\label{lesson:MR-W06-kha}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{ka} with your hand in front of your mouth. Now say it again and push the air out after it. That second sound has its own letter.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\mr{ख}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\mr{ख}} is \emph{kha}: \textbf{\mr{क}} said with a puff of breath released after it. Marathi keeps the two apart the way English keeps \emph{pin} and \emph{bin} apart — swap them and you have a different word.

The shape is not \mr{क} with a mark added; it is its own letter. Draw the left loop, then the upright with its foot, then the headline across the top. You will need it for \emph{khāṇe}, \textquotedblleft{}to eat\textquotedblright{}.

\subsection*{Writing — observe and trace}
Trace \textbf{\mr{ख}} twice with the model visible. Say \emph{ka}, then \emph{kha}, as your pen finishes each one, and listen for the puff that only the second has.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
\emph{ka} or \emph{kha} — which one moves the air? (\emph{\textbf{kha}}.)

Source: \href{https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Deva-\%E0\%A4\%96-order.gif}{Opiaterein, Devanagari kha stroke animation}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ga]{\mr{ग} — the same place, with the voice on}

\label{lesson:MR-W06-ga}



\begin{quote}
Put two fingers on your throat and say \emph{ka}, then \emph{ga}. The place in your mouth does not move. Something else switches on.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\mr{ग}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\mr{ग}} is \emph{ga}: the same back-of-the-mouth closure as \textbf{\mr{क}}, made with the voice running. That is the only difference, and your fingers felt it a moment ago.

The shape is a single curve that swings down and left from the headline and finishes with a small tail on the right. It is the first letter of \emph{gāv}, \textquotedblleft{}village\textquotedblright{}, and it sits inside \emph{sāṅgṇe}, \textquotedblleft{}to tell\textquotedblright{} — a verb this book uses long before it shows you this letter.

\subsection*{Writing — guided copy}
Copy \textbf{\mr{ग}} twice with the model visible. Then write \textbf{\mr{ख}} once from memory beside it, and check the two are not the same shape.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of \emph{ka} and \emph{ga} switches the voice on? (\emph{\textbf{ga}}.)

Source: \href{https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Deva-\%E0\%A4\%97-order.gif}{Opiaterein, Devanagari ga stroke animation}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[gha]{\mr{घ} — voice and breath together}

\label{lesson:MR-W06-gha}



\begin{quote}
You have the puff, and you have the voice. Now do both in one sound.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\mr{घ}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\mr{घ}} is \emph{gha}: voiced like \textbf{\mr{ग}}, breathy like \textbf{\mr{ख}}. Four letters now sit at the same place in your mouth, and only voice and breath tell them apart:

\textbf{\mr{क}} plain · \textbf{\mr{ख}} breath · \textbf{\mr{ग}} voice · \textbf{\mr{घ}} voice and breath.

You already say this letter. \emph{Kāḷjī ghyā}, \textquotedblleft{}take care\textquotedblright{}, ends in it, and so does \emph{gheṇe}, \textquotedblleft{}to take\textquotedblright{}. Draw the left bowl, then the right stem, then the headline.

\subsection*{Writing — delayed copy}
Look at \textbf{\mr{घ}} for five seconds, cover it, and write it once. Uncover and check it against \textbf{\mr{ग}}: the bowl on the left is what you are looking for.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Of \emph{ka, kha, ga, gha} — which one has both? (\emph{\textbf{gha}}.)

Source: \href{https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Deva-\%E0\%A4\%98-order.gif}{Opiaterein, Devanagari gha stroke animation}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ca]{\mr{च} — one letter, two Marathi sounds}

\label{lesson:MR-W06-ca}



\begin{quote}
Move forward in your mouth: from the back, where \emph{ka} lives, to the roof, right behind your teeth.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\mr{च}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\mr{च}} is \emph{ca}, close to English \emph{ch} in \emph{church}. Marathi does something Hindi does not: in many words it says this letter as \textbf{ts}, the sound at the end of English \emph{cats}. \emph{Cār}, \textquotedblleft{}four\textquotedblright{}, is one of them.

One letter, two pronunciations, and no mark on the page to tell you which — that is a thing you learn word by word. The shape is a bowl opening to the right, hung under the headline with a short stem.

\subsection*{Writing — guided copy}
Copy \textbf{\mr{च}} twice with the model visible. Say \emph{ca} on the first and \emph{tsa} on the second, so the hand learns that one shape carries both.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many sounds does \textbf{\mr{च}} carry in Marathi? (\textbf{Two.})

Source: \href{https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Deva-\%E0\%A4\%9A-order.gif}{Opiaterein, Devanagari ca stroke animation}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[cha]{\mr{छ} — the palate, with the breath let out}

\label{lesson:MR-W06-cha}



\begin{quote}
The same pair you learned at the back of the mouth happens again at the roof of it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\mr{छ}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\mr{छ}} is \emph{chha}: \textbf{\mr{च}} with the breath released, exactly the step that took you from \textbf{\mr{क}} to \textbf{\mr{ख}}. Devanagari does this all the way down the alphabet — plain, breathy, voiced, voiced-and-breathy — which is why learning one row teaches you how to hear the next.

The shape is a closed loop with a tail curving away below. It carries \emph{vicāraṇe} in some spellings and stands at the head of \emph{chān}, \textquotedblleft{}nice\textquotedblright{}.

\subsection*{Writing — observe and trace}
Trace \textbf{\mr{छ}} twice, then trace \textbf{\mr{च}} once beside it. Point at the closed loop: that is what the breath costs you on the page.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of \textbf{\mr{च}} and \textbf{\mr{छ}} releases the breath? (\textbf{\mr{छ}}.)

Source: \href{https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Deva-\%E0\%A4\%9B-order.gif}{Opiaterein, Devanagari cha stroke animation}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ja]{\mr{ज} — voice at the palate}

\label{lesson:MR-W06-ja}



\begin{quote}
Fingers on the throat again. Say \emph{ca}, then \emph{ja}. Same roof, voice on.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\mr{ज}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\mr{ज}} is \emph{ja}, and it shadows \textbf{\mr{च}} exactly: where a word says \textbf{\mr{च}} as \emph{ts}, it usually says \textbf{\mr{ज}} as \emph{dz}. The two travel together.

You need it for \emph{jāṇe}, \textquotedblleft{}to go\textquotedblright{}, and it hides inside \emph{kāḷjī}, \textquotedblleft{}care\textquotedblright{}, in the phrase you already use for goodbye. Draw the top stroke, the middle knot, and the descending stem under the headline.

\subsection*{Writing — delayed copy}
Look at \textbf{\mr{ज}} for five seconds, cover it, and write it once. Then retrieve the names of the two letters before it in this chapter.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\mr{ज}} become where \textbf{\mr{च}} becomes \emph{ts}? (\emph{\textbf{dz}}.)

Source: \href{https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Deva-\%E0\%A4\%9C-order.gif}{Opiaterein, Devanagari ja stroke animation}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[jha]{\mr{झ} — the letter inside \emph{mājhe}}

\label{lesson:MR-W06-jha}



\begin{quote}
One more of the four-way sets, and this one closes a word you have been saying since your first introduction.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\mr{झ}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\mr{झ}} is \emph{jha}: voiced like \textbf{\mr{ज}}, breathy like \textbf{\mr{छ}}. The palate now has its full four, in the same order the back of your mouth did.

This is the letter sitting in the middle of \emph{mājhe}, \textquotedblleft{}my\textquotedblright{} — \textbf{\mr{माझे}} — a word this book taught you to say long before it taught you to read it. Every sign in that word is now yours.

\subsection*{Writing — guided copy}
Copy \textbf{\mr{माझे}} twice with the model visible, naming each sign as you form it: \emph{ma}, long \emph{ā}, \emph{jha}, \emph{e}-mark. This is the first whole word this runway has made writable.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which sign in \textbf{\mr{माझे}} did you learn today? (\textbf{\mr{झ}}.)

Source: \href{https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Deva-\%E0\%A4\%9D-order.gif}{Opiaterein, Devanagari jha stroke animation}.
\end{tcolorbox}
